{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_bdrk_01Ay3Q63HNfn7DYVY9ebTfKM","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# Planning Guidance and Checklists\n2\t\n3\tUse the sections that are relevant. These are thinking aids, not forms to fill in. Skip items that clearly don't apply, and go deeper wherever the hard parts are.\n4\t\n5\t## 1. Discovery questions\n6\t\n7\tChoose the questions whose answers would change the design. If you can't ask, choose a default and record it as an assumption.\n8\t\n9\t- Who are the users, how many are there, and where are they? Is the system internal, B2B, or consumer-facing?\n10\t- What is the busiest realistic hour? How much data arrives each day, and how much is kept in total?\n11\t- What is the cost of downtime, of losing data, and of returning a wrong answer? These answers set the reliability and correctness targets.\n12\t- Is the system single-tenant or multi-tenant? Do tenants need their data isolated?\n13\t- What data is regulated or sensitive (personal, health, payment, or confidential data)? Are there residency rules?\n14\t- What must the system integrate with? Are those systems reliable and documented, and who owns them?\n15\t- What stack, cloud, and tooling are already in use or required by the organisation?\n16\t- How many engineers are there, what are their strengths, and how much operational work can they take on?\n17\t- Is there a fixed date? What is the smallest release that would still be valuable?\n18\t- What has been tried before, and why didn't it work?\n19\t\n20\t## 2. Making quality attributes measurable\n21\t\n22\t| Attribute | Express it as |\n23\t|---|---|\n24\t| Latency | Percentile at a given load, e.g. p95 < 250 ms at 100 rps |\n25\t| Availability | Percentage over a window plus maintenance policy, e.g. 99.9% monthly |\n26\t| Recovery | Maximum time to restore and maximum acceptable data loss |\n27\t| Throughput | Sustained and peak rates, with expected growth |\n28\t| Correctness | Error budget or accuracy threshold on a defined evaluation set |\n29\t| Cost | Monthly run cost ceiling, or cost per user, request, or task |\n30\t| Security | Named threats that must be mitigated, plus compliance obligations |\n31\t| Evolvability | The changes that must be cheap, e.g. \"add a new payment provider in under a week\" |\n32\t| Time to market | The date by which a specific capability must be live |\n33\t\n34\tIf a target was invented, label it as an assumption and say how it will be confirmed.\n35\t\n36\t## 3. Decomposition heuristics\n37\t\n38\t- Draw boundaries around business capabilities and the data they own, not around technical layers.\n39\t- Things that change together belong together. Things that change for different reasons should be separated.\n40\t- Each piece of data should have exactly one writer. Shared writable tables between components are a warning sign.\n41\t- Split into separately deployed services only when there is a clear reason: different scaling needs, separate team ownership, different security zones, or different release cadences. Otherwise keep modules inside one deployable unit, with boundaries enforced in code.\n42\t- Keep synchronous call chains short. Use asynchronous messaging where work can be delayed or must survive outages. Accept that this brings eventual consistency and harder debugging.\n43\t- Wrap each external dependency behind your own interface, so it can be replaced, faked in tests, and protected from failures.\n44\t- Check every boundary with one question: can this component be tested and changed without coordinating with the others?\n45\t\n46\t## 4. Data checklist\n47\t\n48\t- Which component is the system of record for each entity?\n49\t- Which operations need atomicity, and do they cross component boundaries? If so, plan for idempotent steps, compensating actions, or an outbox pattern for publishing events reliably.\n50\t- What are the main read and write paths, and which indexes, caches, or read models do they require?\n51\t- How will the schema change without downtime? Use additive changes first, a backfill, a switch of reads, and only then removal of the old structure.\n52\t- What are the retention and deletion obligations, including user deletion requests and legal holds?\n53\t- What are the backup frequency, the restore targets, and the date of the last tested restore?\n54\t- Which fields are sensitive, and are they encrypted, masked in logs, and access-controlled?\n55\t- How will production-like test data be produced without copying sensitive data?\n56\t\n57\t## 5. Choosing technology\n58\t\n59\t- Start with what the team already knows and what the organisation already runs.\n60\t- Prefer managed services when the team is small or operational appetite is low.\n61\t- Before adopting something new, name the driver it satisfies that the existing option can't, and include the cost of learning it and running it.\n62\t- Check for limits that could stop you later: licensing, quotas, regional availability, maximum sizes, rate limits, and whether you can get your data out.\n63\t- Note any decision that ties you deeply to one vendor, and record what leaving would cost.\n64\t- Avoid adopting several new technologies in the same milestone, because it makes failures hard to diagnose.\n65\t\n66\t## 6. Sequencing heuristics\n67\t\n68\t- **First slice:** pick the most representative user scenario and build only enough of each layer to complete it, deployed through the real pipeline to a real environment. Use hard-coded or stubbed pieces freely, but list them.\n69\t- **Spikes:** each one has a question, a time box (typically one to five days), something you can examine at the end, and a result that would change the plan. Schedule them before work that depends on their answers.\n70\t- **Critical path:** find the longest chain of dependent work and start it first. Look for long-lead items such as vendor access, security reviews, procurement, data-sharing agreements, and quota increases. Request them on day one.\n71\t- **Parallel work:** once the interfaces are agreed, independent components can be built at the same time against contracts or fakes.\n72\t- **Milestone size:** aim for milestones that take a few weeks at most and end in something you can demonstrate. Long milestones hide risk.\n73\t- **Hardening:** don't leave all security, performance, and operational work to a final phase. Build each in when its component is built, then verify it before launch.\n74\t- **Order of migrations:** build the new path, run it in parallel or shadow mode, compare results, move traffic over gradually, and only then retire the old path.\n75\t\n76\t## 7. Writing actionable tasks\n77\t\n78\tA good task has a verb, a specific deliverable, a location, and a \"done when\" condition that someone else can check.\n79\t\n80\t- Weak: \"Implement auth.\"\n81\t- Strong: \"Add OIDC login with the organisation's identity provider in `services/api/auth/`. Map provider groups to the `admin` and `member` roles. Done when an integration test logs in a test user from each group and receives the correct permissions.\"\n82\t- Weak: \"Set up monitoring.\"\n83\t- Strong: \"Emit request count, error rate, and p95 latency per endpoint from the API to the existing metrics stack. Add an alert when the error rate exceeds 2% for 5 minutes. Done when a deliberately injected failure in staging triggers the alert.\"\n84\t\n85\tKeep each task to a few days of work at most. Split anything larger.\n86\t\n87\t## 8. Security checklist\n88\t\n89\t- Identity: how users and services authenticate, and where sessions or tokens are checked.\n90\t- Authorisation: the permission model (roles, attributes, or ownership), enforced on the server side for every request.\n91\t- Secrets: stored in a secret manager, never in code or images, and rotatable.\n92\t- Encryption in transit everywhere. Encryption at rest for sensitive stores.\n93\t- Input validation and output encoding at every trust boundary. Parameterised queries.\n94\t- Least privilege for service accounts, infrastructure roles, and AI tool permissions.\n95\t- Dependency and image scanning in CI. A plan for applying patches.\n96\t- Audit logs for security-relevant actions, protected from tampering.\n97\t- The three to five most likely threats for this specific system, each paired with a mitigation.\n98\t\n99\t## 9. Reliability and operations checklist\n100\t\n101\t- A timeout on every network call, retries with backoff and jitter only for idempotent operations, and circuit breaking for fragile dependencies.\n102\t- Idempotency keys for operations that may be retried or delivered twice.\n103\t- Backpressure and queue limits, plus dead-letter handling and a process for reprocessing failed messages.\n104\t- Health checks that reflect whether the system can actually serve requests, not just whether the process is running.\n105\t- Alerts based on symptoms users would notice, each linked to a runbook.\n106\t- Structured logs with correlation IDs that can be followed across components.\n107\t- Deployments that are automated, repeatable, and reversible, with an explicit rollback procedure.\n108\t- A capacity plan and a load test at or above the expected peak before launch.\n109\t- Clear ownership: who is on call, how incidents are handled, and who approves changes.\n110\t\n111\t## 10. AI and agentic systems checklist\n112\t\n113\t- **Evaluation first:** a representative, versioned evaluation set with clear pass criteria, run automatically whenever prompts, models, or tools change. Include adversarial and edge cases.\n114\t- **Simplest design that passes:** start with one model call or a fixed pipeline. Add autonomy, planning loops, or multiple agents only when evaluations show they are needed.\n115\t- **Model choice:** weigh quality, latency, cost, context size, and data-handling terms. Keep model access behind an interface so models can be swapped.\n116\t- **Prompts and configuration:** under version control, reviewed, and tied to evaluation results.\n117\t- **Tools:** narrow, well-described interfaces with validated arguments, least-privilege credentials, and dry-run or confirmation modes for actions that can't be undone.\n118\t- **Limits:** a maximum number of steps, a token and spend budget per task, wall-clock timeouts, and loop detection.\n119\t- **Human oversight:** approval points before irreversible or high-impact actions, and a clear way to hand off to a person.\n120\t- **Untrusted input:** treat retrieved documents, tool outputs, and user content as possible injected instructions. Isolate them, and never let them grant new permissions.\n121\t- **Grounding:** for retrieval-based designs, plan how documents are ingested, split into chunks, and refreshed, along with access control on retrieved content and measurement of retrieval quality.\n122\t- **Failure handling:** fallbacks for when the model is slow, unavailable, wrong, or refuses to answer, and degraded modes that still work for users.\n123\t- **Observability:** log inputs, outputs, tool calls, latency, and cost for each step, with redaction of sensitive data. Sample production traffic back into the evaluation set.\n124\t- **Data handling:** what is sent to model providers, how long they keep it, and whether it is allowed to be sent.\n125\t\n126\t## 11. Infrastructure checklist\n127\t\n128\t- All resources defined as code, reviewed, and applied through a pipeline, with no manual changes in production.\n129\t- Environments kept as consistent as possible, with the differences between them stated openly.\n130\t- Remote infrastructure state with locking. State split so a single change can only affect a limited area.\n131\t- Identity, account or project layout, and network design planned first, because they are the hardest to change later.\n132\t- Changes promoted from development to staging to production, with automated checks at each stage.\n133\t- Quotas, limits, and regional capacity checked early.\n134\t- Cost tagging, budgets, and alerts.\n135\t- Backup, disaster recovery, and failover procedures, each tested.\n136\t\n137\t## 12. Brownfield and migration checklist\n138\t\n139\t- List what the current system actually does, including undocumented behaviour that users rely on.\n140\t- Find a point where requests or data can be split between the old and new systems.\n141\t- Decide whether to migrate incrementally, by feature, tenant, or traffic percentage, or all at once, and justify the choice.\n142\t- Plan how data stays in sync while both systems run, and how the two will be reconciled.\n143\t- Define switchover criteria and the point after which rollback is no longer possible.\n144\t- Plan when the old system will be retired. Old systems that are never retired double the operational cost.\n145\t\n146\t## 13. Common failure modes to check against\n147\t\n148\t- The architecture serves a scale or level of flexibility nobody asked for.\n149\t- Weeks of foundation work with nothing demonstrable at the end.\n150\t- Integration and deployment attempted for the first time near the deadline.\n151\t- Several components writing to the same data, so ownership is unclear.\n152\t- No plan for schema changes, backfills, or rollback.\n153\t- AI behaviour assumed rather than measured.\n154\t- Long-lead dependencies discovered late.\n155\t- Estimates given as single numbers with no stated assumptions.\n156\t- Decisions presented as lists of options with no recommendation.\n157\t"}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"62c71bd1-9fca-486d-bf25-73c14c67d4d2","uuid":"d86c901c-605d-40f5-8c02-84b25dbff1af","timestamp":"2026-10-03T00:04:15.004Z","tool_use_result":{"type":"text","file":{"filePath":"C:\\Users\\nrvhari\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\dfa-eval\\2026-10-03-pilot-core\\plugins\\p2ab33809\\skills\\architecture-planner\\reference\\guidance.md","content":"# Planning Guidance and Checklists\n\nUse the sections that are relevant. Discovery questions\n\nChoose the questions whose answers would change the design. If you can't ask, choose a default and record it as an assumption.\n\n- Who are the users, how many are there, and where are they? Is the system internal, B2B, or consumer-facing?\n- What is the busiest realistic hour? How much data arrives each day, and how much is kept in total?\n- What is the cost of downtime, of losing data, and of returning a wrong answer? These answers set the reliability and correctness targets.\n- Is the system single-tenant or multi-tenant? Do tenants need their data isolated?\n- What data is regulated or sensitive (personal, health, payment, or confidential data)? Are there residency rules?\n- What must the system integrate with? Are those systems reliable and documented, and who owns them?\n- What stack, cloud, and tooling are already in use or required by the organisation?\n- How many engineers are there, what are their strengths, and how much operational work can they take on?\n- Is there a fixed date? What is the smallest release that would still be valuable?\n- What has been tried before, and why didn't it work?\n\n## 2. Making quality attributes measurable\n\n| Attribute | Express it as |\n|---|---|\n| Latency | Percentile at a given load, e.g. p95 < 250 ms at 100 rps |\n| Availability | Percentage over a window plus maintenance policy, e.g. 99.9% monthly |\n| Recovery | Maximum time to restore and maximum acceptable data loss |\n| Throughput | Sustained and peak rates, with expected growth |\n| Correctness | Error budget or accuracy threshold on a defined evaluation set |\n| Cost | Monthly run cost ceiling, or cost per user, request, or task |\n| Security | Named threats that must be mitigated, plus compliance obligations |\n| Evolvability | The changes that must be cheap, e.g. \"add a new payment provider in under a week\" |\n| Time to market | The date by which a specific capability must be live |\n\nIf a target was invented, label it as an assumption and say how it will be confirmed.\n\n## 3. Decomposition heuristics\n\n- Draw boundaries around business capabilities and the data they own, not around technical layers.\n- Things that change together belong together. Things that change for different reasons should be separated.\n- Each piece of data should have exactly one writer. Shared writable tables between components are a warning sign.\n- Split into separately deployed services only when there is a clear reason: different scaling needs, separate team ownership, different security zones, or different release cadences. Accept that this brings eventual consistency and harder debugging.\n- Wrap each external dependency behind your own interface, so it can be replaced, faked in tests, and protected from failures.\n- Check every boundary with one question: can this component be tested and changed without coordinating with the others?\n\n## 4. Data checklist\n\n- Which component is the system of record for each entity?\n- Which operations need atomicity, and do they cross component boundaries? If so, plan for idempotent steps, compensating actions, or an outbox pattern for publishing events reliably.\n- What are the main read and write paths, and which indexes, caches, or read models do they require?\n- How will the schema change without downtime? Use additive changes first, a backfill, a switch of reads, and only then removal of the old structure.\n- What are the retention and deletion obligations, including user deletion requests and legal holds?\n- What are the backup frequency, the restore targets, and the date of the last tested restore?\n- Which fields are sensitive, and are they encrypted, masked in logs, and access-controlled?\n- How will production-like test data be produced without copying sensitive data?\n\n## 5. Choosing technology\n\n- Start with what the team already knows and what the organisation already runs.\n- Prefer managed services when the team is small or operational appetite is low.\n- Before adopting something new, name the driver it satisfies that the existing option can't, and include the cost of learning it and running it.\n- Check for limits that could stop you later: licensing, quotas, regional availability, maximum sizes, rate limits, and whether you can get your data out.\n- Note any decision that ties you deeply to one vendor, and record what leaving would cost.\n- Avoid adopting several new technologies in the same milestone, because it makes failures hard to diagnose.\n\n## 6. Use hard-coded or stubbed pieces freely, but list them.\n- **Spikes:** each one has a question, a time box (typically one to five days), something you can examine at the end, and a result that would change the plan. Schedule them before work that depends on their answers.\n- **Critical path:** find the longest chain of dependent work and start it first. Look for long-lead items such as vendor access, security reviews, procurement, data-sharing agreements, and quota increases. Request them on day one.\n- **Parallel work:** once the interfaces are agreed, independent components can be built at the same time against contracts or fakes.\n- **Milestone size:** aim for milestones that take a few weeks at most and end in something you can demonstrate. Long milestones hide risk.\n- **Hardening:** don't leave all security, performance, and operational work to a final phase. Build each in when its component is built, then verify it before launch.\n- **Order of migrations:** build the new path, run it in parallel or shadow mode, compare results, move traffic over gradually, and only then retire the old path.\n\n## 7. Writing actionable tasks\n\nA good task has a verb, a specific deliverable, a location, and a \"done when\" condition that someone else can check.\n\n- Weak: \"Implement auth.\"\n- Strong: \"Add OIDC login with the organisation's identity provider in `services/api/auth/`. Add an alert when the error rate exceeds 2% for 5 minutes. Done when a deliberately injected failure in staging triggers the alert.\"\n\nKeep each task to a few days of work at most. Security checklist\n\n- Identity: how users and services authenticate, and where sessions or tokens are checked.\n- Authorisation: the permission model (roles, attributes, or ownership), enforced on the server side for every request.\n- Secrets: stored in a secret manager, never in code or images, and rotatable.\n- Encryption in transit everywhere. Encryption at rest for sensitive stores.\n- Input validation and output encoding at every trust boundary. Parameterised queries.\n- Least privilege for service accounts, infrastructure roles, and AI tool permissions.\n- Dependency and image scanning in CI. A plan for applying patches.\n- Audit logs for security-relevant actions, protected from tampering.\n- The three to five most likely threats for this specific system, each paired with a mitigation.\n\n## 9. Reliability and operations checklist\n\n- A timeout on every network call, retries with backoff and jitter only for idempotent operations, and circuit breaking for fragile dependencies.\n- Idempotency keys for operations that may be retried or delivered twice.\n- Backpressure and queue limits, plus dead-letter handling and a process for reprocessing failed messages.\n- Health checks that reflect whether the system can actually serve requests, not just whether the process is running.\n- Alerts based on symptoms users would notice, each linked to a runbook.\n- Structured logs with correlation IDs that can be followed across components.\n- Deployments that are automated, repeatable, and reversible, with an explicit rollback procedure.\n- A capacity plan and a load test at or above the expected peak before launch.\n- Clear ownership: who is on call, how incidents are handled, and who approves changes.\n\n## 10. AI and agentic systems checklist\n\n- **Evaluation first:** a representative, versioned evaluation set with clear pass criteria, run automatically whenever prompts, models, or tools change. Include adversarial and edge cases.\n- **Simplest design that passes:** start with one model call or a fixed pipeline. Add autonomy, planning loops, or multiple agents only when evaluations show they are needed.\n- **Model choice:** weigh quality, latency, cost, context size, and data-handling terms. Keep model access behind an interface so models can be swapped.\n- **Prompts and configuration:** under version control, reviewed, and tied to evaluation results.\n- **Tools:** narrow, well-described interfaces with validated arguments, least-privilege credentials, and dry-run or confirmation modes for actions that can't be undone.\n- **Limits:** a maximum number of steps, a token and spend budget per task, wall-clock timeouts, and loop detection.\n- **Human oversight:** approval points before irreversible or high-impact actions, and a clear way to hand off to a person.\n- **Untrusted input:** treat retrieved documents, tool outputs, and user content as possible injected instructions. Isolate them, and never let them grant new permissions.\n- **Grounding:** for retrieval-based designs, plan how documents are ingested, split into chunks, and refreshed, along with access control on retrieved content and measurement of retrieval quality.\n- **Failure handling:** fallbacks for when the model is slow, unavailable, wrong, or refuses to answer, and degraded modes that still work for users.\n- **Observability:** log inputs, outputs, tool calls, latency, and cost for each step, with redaction of sensitive data. Sample production traffic back into the evaluation set.\n- **Data handling:** what is sent to model providers, how long they keep it, and whether it is allowed to be sent.\n\n## 11. Infrastructure checklist\n\n- All resources defined as code, reviewed, and applied through a pipeline, with no manual changes in production.\n- Environments kept as consistent as possible, with the differences between them stated openly.\n- Remote infrastructure state with locking. State split so a single change can only affect a limited area.\n- Identity, account or project layout, and network design planned first, because they are the hardest to change later.\n- Changes promoted from development to staging to production, with automated checks at each stage.\n- Quotas, limits, and regional capacity checked early.\n- Cost tagging, budgets, and alerts.\n- Backup, disaster recovery, and failover procedures, each tested.\n\n## 12. Brownfield and migration checklist\n\n- List what the current system actually does, including undocumented behaviour that users rely on.\n- Find a point where requests or data can be split between the old and new systems.\n- Decide whether to migrate incrementally, by feature, tenant, or traffic percentage, or all at once, and justify the choice.\n- Plan how data stays in sync while both systems run, and how the two will be reconciled.\n- Define switchover criteria and the point after which rollback is no longer possible.\n- Plan when the old system will be retired. Old systems that are never retired double the operational cost.\n\n## 13. Common failure modes to check against\n\n- The architecture serves a scale or level of flexibility nobody asked for.\n- Weeks of foundation work with nothing demonstrable at the end.\n- Integration and deployment attempted for the first time near the deadline.\n- Several components writing to the same data, so ownership is unclear.\n- No plan for schema changes, backfills, or rollback.\n- AI behaviour assumed rather than measured.\n- Long-lead dependencies discovered late.\n- Estimates given as single numbers with no stated assumptions.\n- Decisions presented as lists of options with no recommendation.\n","numLines":157,"startLine":1,"totalLines":157}}}

Current State\n34\t\n35\tWhat exists today that this work touches: relevant code, services, data stores, infrastructure, and processes. {"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-opus-5-5","id":"msg_bdrk_tq4pigmqqswdtazcbkoznkofpsa2xgirj3vhn4hq7chbub6f7dbq","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"text","text":"# Architecture and Build Plan: Real-Time Collaborative Document Editor\n\n> **Context note.** The workspace has nothing in it except a README saying it is intentionally empty, so this is a greenfield plan. You asked me to order the build and left the details open, so I went ahead without asking questions first. Every assumption is marked **[A]** and collected in Section 5. Because the request is mostly about sequencing, Sections 12–13 carry the most detail and the rest is kept short.\n\n---\n\n## 1. Summary\n\n- **What:** a web-based rich-text editor like a smaller Google Docs, for teams inside workspaces (B2B, multi-tenant) **[A]**. Several people edit the same document at once and see each other's edits and cursors live.\n- **Shape:** a TypeScript monorepo with two deployable processes. The **API service** (REST) handles accounts, documents and permissions. The **Collab service** (WebSocket) handles live sync. Both use one Postgres database. Redis is added in M3 so more than one Collab instance can run. Clients merge edits with a **CRDT** (a data structure where concurrent edits merge automatically and always end up the same on every copy), so typing never waits on the network.\n- **Key decisions:**\n  1. Use **Yjs**, an existing CRDT library, rather than building our own merge algorithm or using operational transformation (OT).\n  2. Use **Tiptap/ProseMirror** as the editor.\n  3. **Self-host Hocuspocus**, an open-source Yjs WebSocket server, rather than paying for a managed collaboration backend.\n  4. Store edits in Postgres as an **append-only log of updates with periodic compaction into snapshots**. Clients also keep a local copy, so an edit is lost only if the server and the client fail together.\n  5. The API issues **short-lived per-document tokens**, and revocations are pushed to open connections.\n- **First milestone (about 3 weeks):** a working slice in staging. Two real users log in, create a document, edit it at the same time, and lose nothing when the Collab server is killed. CI also runs a test that checks all copies converge. Three spikes (short, time-boxed experiments) answer the questions that could change the plan: durable save confirmation, fan-out capacity, and document-schema evolution.\n- **Top risks:** edits lost or copies drifting apart without anyone noticing; one busy document overloading a server; old clients corrupting documents after a schema change; editor edge cases (IME input, paste) eating the schedule.\n\n## 2. Context and Goals\n\n- **Problem:** teams want to write together live, without emailing files around or locking documents. **[A]** No existing tool needs replacing.\n- **Goals:** concurrent editing with live cursors; no acknowledged edit ever lost; sharing at owner/editor/viewer level; comments and version history by GA.\n- **Non-goals for v1:** native mobile apps; full offline-first editing (short disconnects are handled); suggestion/track-changes mode; spreadsheets or slides; end-to-end encryption; multi-region; Word or Google Docs import; AI features.\n- **Success measures:** zero confirmed lost-edit incidents; p95 time for a remote edit to appear under 300 ms; at least 60% of beta workspaces with a weekly co-edited document **[A]**; the team runs on its own product by M2.\n\n## 3. Drivers, Requirements, and Constraints\n\n**Ranked quality attributes**\n\n| # | Attribute | Measurable target | Why it matters |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| 1 | Data integrity and convergence | 0 lost edits once acknowledged. All copies converge to the same state. Server-side data-loss window ≤ 250 ms, and clients resend anything the server lost | Losing someone's writing destroys trust immediately and permanently |\n| 2 | Collaboration latency | Local keystroke under 16 ms (never waits on the network). Remote edit visible p95 < 300 ms in the same region with 20 editors per document **[A]** | Collaboration feels broken above roughly half a second |\n| 3 | Access control and tenant isolation | No cross-tenant reads. Viewers cannot write. Revoked access cut off within 5 s of the change | Document content is customers' confidential data |\n| 4 | Time to market | Internal dogfooding by week ~7, external beta by week ~11, GA by week ~16 **[A]** | Sets how much we build ourselves versus reuse |\n| 5 | Operability and cost | One on-call rotation from the build team. Under about $1.5k/month infrastructure at 10k daily active users **[A]**. 99.9% monthly availability for editing | A small team runs it |\n\n**Key functional requirements:** live co-editing of rich text (headings, lists, links, code, then tables and images); presence and cursors; undo that only undoes your own changes; sharing; a save-state indicator (\"Saved\", \"Saving…\", \"Offline – kept on this device\"); comments; version history.\n\n**Constraints [A]:** 4 full-stack engineers who are strong in TypeScript, React, Node and Postgres; AWS (or whichever cloud the organisation already uses); an OIDC identity provider; one region; no regulated data beyond ordinary confidential business content.\n\n**Hard parts**\n\n1. **Durable save without slowing typing.** Telling the user \"saved\" is a promise. It needs a server confirmation that is tied to a real database commit.\n2. **Fan-out under load.** One document with 50 active typists generates about 12k outbound messages per second.\n3. **Document-schema evolution.** An old client that receives a node type it doesn't recognise may fail or rewrite content, and in a CRDT that rewrite spreads to everyone.\n4. **Authorisation on long-lived connections.** The permission is checked when the connection opens, but it has to be enforced for as long as the connection stays open.\n5. **Proving convergence.** Bugs where copies drift apart don't show up in normal manual testing.\n\n## 4. Current State\n\nThe workspace is empty (`README.md`: \"no existing code, documentation, configuration, or data\"). There are no conventions to follow. This plan sets them: a pnpm monorepo, strict TypeScript, SQL migrations, Terraform, and GitHub Actions **[A]**.\n\n## 5. Assumptions and Open Questions\n\n| Assumption | Impact if wrong | How / when validated |\n|---|---|---|\n| B2B, multi-tenant workspaces, 10k daily users, 2k peak concurrent connections | The scale target could change by 10× in either direction | Product owner, week 1 |\n| Typically 1–5 editors per document, at most 50 editors and 200 viewers | Spike S2 sizing; per-document caps | Product owner, week 1; S2 |\n| Self-hosting is acceptable (content must not go to a third-party sync vendor) | If not, buying a managed backend could save about 4–6 weeks | Week 1 (decision D2) |\n| Team of 4 with TypeScript/React/Node/Postgres skills | Sizes in Section 12 | Week 1 |\n| Desktop browsers only (Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari) | Mobile input handling adds weeks | Product owner, week 1 |\n| AWS in one region with OIDC; the identity-provider tenant can be obtained in under 1 week | Long-lead item on the critical path | Request on day 1 |\n| Short disconnects (minutes) are enough; true offline is not needed | Offline-first changes conflict UX and storage | Product owner, M1 |\n\n**Open questions** are listed at the end of this reply. Each has a default. All must be settled by the M1 exit.\n\n## 6. Architecture Overview\n\n```mermaid\nflowchart LR\n  subgraph Browser[\"Browser (untrusted)\"]\n    W[Web app: React + Tiptap + Yjs<br/>IndexedDB local copy]\n  end\n  subgraph Cloud[\"Our cloud account (trust boundary)\"]\n    LB[Load balancer / TLS]\n    API[API service<br/>REST, Fastify]\n    COL[Collab service<br/>Hocuspocus WebSocket]\n    PG[(Postgres)]\n    R[(Redis — from M3)]\n    S3[(Object storage — from M3)]\n  end\n  IDP[OIDC identity provider]\n  W -- HTTPS REST --> LB --> API\n  W -- WSS Yjs sync + awareness --> LB --> COL\n  W -- presigned upload --> S3\n  API -- OIDC --> IDP\n  API --> PG\n  COL --> PG\n  API -- permission-changed events --> COL\n  COL <--> R\n```\n\nThe web app edits a local Yjs document. Every change is applied on the spot, written to IndexedDB, and sent to the Collab service. The Collab service relays changes to everyone else in the document, appends them to Postgres in batches, and confirms the save once the batch has committed. The API owns everything except document content, and it issues the token a client needs to join a document's session. Permission-change events go from the API to the Collab service: Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY in M1–M2, Redis pub/sub from M3.\n\n| Component | Responsibility | Owns data | Exposes | Technology | Depends on |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Web app (`apps/web`) | Editing UI, local copy, presence, save indicator | IndexedDB copy (cache only) | — | React, Vite, Tiptap, Yjs, `@hocuspocus/provider`, `y-indexeddb` | API, Collab |\n| API service (`apps/api`) | Login, workspaces, document metadata, permissions, collab tokens; later comments, versions, attachments | `users`, `workspaces`, `memberships`, `documents`, `document_permissions`, later `comments`, `doc_versions`, `attachments` | REST/JSON `/v1/...` | Node 20+, Fastify, zod | Postgres, identity provider |\n| Collab service (`apps/collab`) | WebSocket sync, awareness (live presence), enforcing permissions on connections, storing content, compaction | `doc_updates`, `doc_snapshots`, `document_projections` | WSS (Yjs sync protocol + stateless messages) | Node 20+, Hocuspocus | Postgres, Redis (M3) |\n| Document schema (`packages/doc-schema`) | One shared definition of allowed nodes and marks, plus the schema version | — | TS library | Tiptap extensions | — |\n| Contracts (`packages/contracts`) | REST types, token claims, event payloads | — | TS library | zod | — |\n\n## 7. Component Details\n\n**Collab service** (the hard component)\n- **Does:** checks the token when a client connects and marks viewer connections read-only on the server; relays updates and awareness; batches updates to Postgres (every 250 ms or 50 updates, whichever comes first); sends a stateless `persisted` message carrying the highest committed sequence number; compacts the log into snapshots; projects the title and plain text into `document_projections`; closes connections when a permission-changed event arrives.\n- **Does not:** decide permissions (the API decides and puts the result in the token), serve REST, or store attachments.\n- **Limits:** messages up to 1 MB; total document state up to 10 MB; 100 connections per document; 300 updates per second per connection. All limits are configurable.\n- **Failure:** on a crash, unflushed updates (≤ 250 ms worth) are lost on the server. Clients reconnect with exponential backoff plus jitter, and the Yjs sync handshake compares what each side has and resends the missing updates. Duplicate updates do no harm because applying a Yjs update twice has no extra effect. On SIGTERM, the service flushes, then closes connections with a \"reconnect\" code. If Postgres is down, it keeps serving from memory, stops sending `persisted` acknowledgements (clients show \"Saving…\"), and buffers up to 256 MB, after which it refuses new document loads.\n- **Scaling:** M1–M2 run one instance. M3 runs at least 2 instances with the Hocuspocus Redis extension. When two instances hold the same document, compaction takes a per-document Postgres advisory lock (a lock keyed to the document ID) so they don't conflict.\n\n**API service:** routine REST CRUD. Every request checks permissions on the server through one `authorize(user, doc, action)` function in `apps/api/src/authz/`. Collab tokens are JWTs with a 10-minute lifetime and claims `{sub, doc, ws, role, minSchema}`, signed with a key from the secret manager.\n\n**Web app:** typing is never blocked. The save indicator is driven by `persisted` acknowledgements and how old the oldest unacknowledged update is. Undo uses `Y.UndoManager` scoped to your own changes. Below `minSchema` the client is forced to reload.\n\n## 8. Data Design\n\n| Entity | Key fields | System of record / writer | Notes |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| `users`, `workspaces`, `memberships` | idp_subject, role admin/member | Postgres / API | |\n| `documents` | id (UUID), workspace_id, created_by, deleted_at, schema_version | Postgres / API | Metadata only |\n| `document_permissions` | document_id, principal (user or workspace), role owner/editor/viewer (+commenter in M4) | Postgres / API | Index on (principal, document) |\n| `doc_updates` | document_id, seq (bigserial), update (bytea), created_at | Postgres / **Collab only** | Append-only. Index on (document_id, seq) |\n| `doc_snapshots` | document_id PK, state (bytea), upto_seq | Postgres / **Collab only** | Load = snapshot + updates where seq > upto_seq |\n| `document_projections` | document_id, title, plaintext, content_updated_at | Postgres / **Collab only**; API reads it | Kept separate so each table has one writer. Later feeds search |\n| `doc_versions` (M4) | document_id, state, label, created_by | Postgres / API (asks Collab for state) | Full-state copies, not Yjs native snapshots |\n| `attachments` (M3) | document_id, s3_key, mime, size | Postgres + S3 / API | Presigned uploads |\n\n- **Consistency:** compaction runs in one transaction: insert the snapshot with `upto_seq`, then delete updates ≤ `upto_seq`, all under the advisory lock. Sharing changes commit before the revoke event is published.\n- **Access patterns:** loading a document is one indexed range scan. The document list reads `document_permissions` joined to `documents` and `document_projections`.\n- **Retention:** soft-deleted documents are hard-deleted after 30 days (all rows plus S3 objects). Compaction triggers when the log exceeds 500 rows or when a document is unloaded.\n- **Backup:** managed point-in-time recovery with 14-day retention. Database RPO 5 minutes, RTO 1 hour. A restore drill is run in M2.\n- **Classification:** content is confidential. It is encrypted at rest (managed) and uses TLS everywhere. **Content is never logged**; logs carry document and user IDs only.\n- **Schema evolution:** database changes are additive first, then backfilled, then old structures removed. Document-schema changes follow the rule in D10.\n\n## 9. Key Flows\n\n**F1: Open a document**\n1. `GET /v1/documents/:id` → API runs `authorize` and returns metadata and a collab token, or 404 (not 403, so it doesn't reveal that the document exists).\n2. The client loads its IndexedDB copy and renders it straight away, then opens WSS and sends the token.\n3. Collab verifies the token signature and that its `doc` claim matches the room, and checks `minSchema`. If the document isn't in memory, it loads the snapshot plus later updates.\n4. Sync handshake (each side sends what the other is missing), then awareness. Target: p95 under 1 s to an editable document for a 1 MB document.\n\n**F2: Edit and save**\n1. Keystroke → ProseMirror transaction → Yjs update. It is applied locally, written to IndexedDB, and sent over the WebSocket.\n2. Collab applies it, relays it to peers (and to Redis from M3), and adds it to the flush buffer.\n3. A flush within 250 ms commits a batch to `doc_updates` and sends `persisted{seq}` → the client shows \"Saved\".\n\n**F3 (failure): the Collab instance crashes mid-session**\n1. The process dies with up to 250 ms of updates not yet written. Clients see the socket close and show \"Reconnecting…\", but editing continues locally.\n2. Reconnects are spread over 0.5–5 s by jitter, so they don't all arrive at once. Loads are limited to 20 concurrent documents per instance.\n3. The sync handshake: the client sends the updates the server lacks, the server writes them, and `persisted` is sent.\n4. Result: no loss unless the client was also closed **and** its IndexedDB was lost before reconnecting. If a tab is closed during the outage, the edits are resent the next time that document is opened in that browser.\n\n**F4: Access revoked mid-session**\n1. The owner removes an editor through `DELETE /v1/documents/:id/permissions/...`, and it commits.\n2. The API publishes `permission_changed{doc,user}`. Collab closes that user's connections with code 4403.\n3. The client asks for a new token, the API refuses, and the client shows \"Access removed\" and deletes its IndexedDB copy. That user's unsynced edits are discarded, which is accepted.\n4. Fallback if the event is lost: the 10-minute token lifetime, checked again on every reconnect, plus a forced reconnect every 10 minutes.\n\n## 10. Key Decisions\n\n| # | Decision | Options considered | Rationale (drivers) | Reversibility | Revisit if |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| D1 | Yjs CRDT | Yjs; OT with ShareDB; ProseMirror central-authority collab; build our own | #1, #2, #4: mature, edits apply locally, duplicates are harmless, good ecosystem. Building our own is a research project | **Hard**: the stored format is Yjs binary | Fine-grained authorship or suggestion mode needs something Yjs can't model |\n| D2 | Self-host Hocuspocus | Hocuspocus; managed (Liveblocks, Tiptap Cloud); custom server on `y-protocols` | #3 data control, #5 cost; the hooks cover auth, persistence and Redis | Medium | **S1 fails** → custom server (+1.5–2 weeks). Team under 3 people or little appetite for operations → buy |\n| D3 | Tiptap (ProseMirror) | Tiptap; Lexical; Slate; Quill | Strict schema, proven `y-prosemirror` binding, extension ecosystem | Hard (tied to D1 format) | — |\n| D4 | Postgres append log + snapshot compaction | Debounced full-state overwrite; snapshots in S3 | #1 small loss window, low write amplification (overwriting a 1 MB document every 2 s is wasteful), one database | Medium | Snapshots regularly over 5 MB → move snapshot blobs to S3 |\n| D5 | Two processes (API, Collab), one repo | Single process; microservices | API deploys (many per day) mustn't drop every editing session. Different scaling profile (long-lived connections, documents held in memory) | Easy | — |\n| D6 | Redis pub/sub for multiple instances (M3) | Route each document to one instance (document affinity) | Supported Hocuspocus extension, works with any load balancer | Medium | Redis throughput or latency becomes the bottleneck in the M3 load test |\n| D7 | API-issued 10-minute JWT + pushed revocation | Collab queries the DB on each connect or message | Keeps permission logic in one place (the API); #3 revocation within 5 s | Easy | — |\n| D8 | Managed OIDC; sessions in httpOnly cookies | Our own password auth | #3, #4 | Medium | Org mandates SSO/SCIM → pull forward |\n| D9 | Version history = full-state copies, Yjs garbage collection on | Yjs native snapshots (need garbage collection off, so documents grow) | Keeps documents small; restore = apply the difference as a new edit | Medium | Users need character-level history |\n| D10 | Document-schema rule: new node types ship **disabled for one release**, then `minSchema` is raised, then they are enabled | Ship and hope | Hard part #3; S3 measures how bad the failure is | — | — |\n\n## 11. Cross-Cutting Concerns\n\n- **Security (M1 outline, M2 complete):** main threats and mitigations:\n  1. Cross-tenant access → `authorize()` on every REST call and checked at token issue; negative tests in CI.\n  2. A viewer sending crafted writes over the WebSocket → server-side read-only flag on the connection; integration test sends raw updates as a viewer and expects rejection.\n  3. Stored XSS through content or paste → schema allowlist, `href` protocol allowlist (http, https, mailto), strict CSP, paste sanitised by parsing it against the schema.\n  4. Revoked user keeps access → F4.\n  5. Denial of service through huge updates or connection floods → the limits in Section 7, per-user connection cap of 20, rate limiting at the load balancer.\n\n  Secrets go in the secret manager. Dependency scanning runs in CI. Sharing changes are written to an audit log table (M2).\n- **Reliability (M2–M3):** 99.9% target for editing. The client's degraded mode keeps local editing working. Every network call has a timeout. The Postgres pool has a circuit breaker. Collab has graceful drain on deploy. The health check verifies the database round-trip, not just that the process is alive.\n- **Observability (M1 basic, M2 alerts):** pino JSON logs with connection and document IDs. Metrics: connections, loaded documents, flush latency and failures, `persisted` lag, document load time, document size. **Synthetic canary (M2):** two headless clients edit a canary document every minute in production. They measure propagation time and check that their copies match, and an alert fires when p95 exceeds 1 s or the copies differ. Clients report \"unsaved for more than 30 s\" events. Alerts: flush failures for over 1 minute, canary failure, unsaved-age p95 over 10 s, connection error rate over 5%.\n- **Performance and capacity:** expected peak is about 600 active typists × 5 updates/s = 3k updates/s in, and about 1.6k batched inserts/s. The bottlenecks to watch are fan-out in one large document, Node event-loop lag, and memory per loaded document. Covered by S2 in M1 and a load test at 2× peak in M3.\n- **Cost [A]:** about $800–1,500/month: 2× Collab and 2× API containers (2 vCPU / 4 GB), a mid-size managed Postgres, a small Redis, load balancer, S3. The main costs are Collab memory and database IOPS. Budget alerts at 80% and 100%.\n- **Operations (M3):** the build team owns it with a weekly on-call rotation. Runbooks for Collab crash loops, a Postgres outage, a stuck compaction, and a \"user reports lost edit\" investigation (rebuild the document from `doc_updates`).\n- **AI-specific concerns:** not applicable; there are no AI components in scope.\n\n## 12. Build Sequence\n\nTeam assumption: 4 engineers. Sizes are rough ranges, not commitments.\n\n| Milestone | Goal / risk cleared | Scope (and exclusions) | Exit criteria (checkable) | Depends on | Size |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| **M1: Walking skeleton + spikes** | Proves the core loop end to end in a real environment. Answers S1–S3 | Monorepo, CI/CD, staging, OIDC login, create/list/open documents (creator-only access), basic rich text, Collab service with append-log persistence, connection indicator, basic metrics, convergence harness. *Excludes:* sharing, cursors, IndexedDB, multiple instances | In staging, 2 users on 2 machines co-edit; Playwright shows propagation in under 1 s; `kill -9` of Collab loses no acknowledged edit; convergence suite (200 seeds) green in CI; S1–S3 write-ups in `docs/decisions/` and this plan updated | Cloud account, identity-provider tenant (day 1) | 2.5–4 wks |\n| **M2: Trustworthy for one team (dogfood)** | Integrity and access control usable every day | Sharing (owner/editor/viewer), read-only enforcement, revocation (F4), cursors and presence, per-user undo, IndexedDB copy + save indicator, compaction, `document_projections`, canary + alerts, audit log, restore drill, `minSchema` gate, spike S4 (large documents) | The team writes all its own documents in it for 1 week with 0 lost edits; viewer-write and cross-tenant tests green; revocation within 5 s; restore drill run within RTO 1 h | M1 | 3–5 wks |\n| **M3: Beta-ready** | Scale, deploy safety, content richness | 2+ Collab instances with Redis, graceful drain, rolling deploys, tables/images (S3)/code blocks, paste sanitisation, limits and rate limits, load test at 2× peak, runbooks, on-call, workspace allowlist flag | Load test: 4k connections and a 50-editor document at p95 < 300 ms; rolling deploy during the load test loses no edits; 3 external beta workspaces onboarded | M2 | 3–6 wks |\n| **M4: GA feature set** | Collaboration features users expect | Comments anchored to text (Yjs relative positions) + commenter role, version history + restore (D9), @mention email notifications, Markdown/PDF export | Beta success measures met; 30 days with 0 lost-edit incidents; security review passed | M3 | 4–7 wks |\n\n**Total:** about 13–22 weeks.\n\n**Critical path:** identity-provider and cloud access (day 1) → **S1 persistence** → Collab persistence → compaction (M2) → multiple instances + drain (M3) → load test → beta. The editor UI (Tiptap schema, UX), the API and sharing, and infra/CI run in parallel against `packages/contracts`.\n\n**Spike S4 (M2, 2 days):** how long do a 200-page document and 50k historical updates take to load, and how large is the stored state? If a load takes over 2 s → compact more aggressively and lower the document size cap.\n\n## 13. First Milestone Task Breakdown\n\nProposed layout: `apps/{web,api,collab}`, `packages/{doc-schema,contracts}`, `db/migrations/`, `infra/`, `tests/{e2e,convergence,load}/`, `docs/decisions/`.\n\n| # | Task | Location | Done when | Order |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| T0 | **Request** cloud account, domain + TLS, and identity-provider tenant | — | Access granted | Day 1 (long lead) |\n| T1 | **Create** pnpm monorepo: strict TS, ESLint, Vitest, workspaces above; You asked me to order the build and left the details open, so I went ahead without asking questions first. Every assumption is marked **[A]** and collected in Section 5. Because the request is mostly about sequencing, Sections 12–13 carry the most detail and the rest is kept short.\n\n---\n\n## 1. Summary\n\n- **What:** a web-based rich-text editor like a smaller Google Docs, for teams inside workspaces (B2B, multi-tenant) **[A]**. Several people edit the same document at once and see each other's edits and cursors live.\n- **Shape:** a TypeScript monorepo with two deployable processes. The **API service** (REST) handles accounts, documents and permissions. The **Collab service** (WebSocket) handles live sync. Both use one Postgres database. Redis is added in M3 so more than one Collab instance can run. Clients merge edits with a **CRDT** (a data structure where concurrent edits merge automatically and always end up the same on every copy), so typing never waits on the network.\n- **Key decisions:**\n  1. Use **Yjs**, an existing CRDT library, rather than building our own merge algorithm or using operational transformation (OT).\n  2. Use **Tiptap/ProseMirror** as the editor.\n  3. **Self-host Hocuspocus**, an open-source Yjs WebSocket server, rather than paying for a managed collaboration backend.\n  4. Store edits in Postgres as an **append-only log of updates with periodic compaction into snapshots**. Clients also keep a local copy, so an edit is lost only if the server and the client fail together.\n  5. The API issues **short-lived per-document tokens**, and revocations are pushed to open connections.\n- **First milestone (about 3 weeks):** a working slice in staging. Two real users log in, create a document, edit it at the same time, and lose nothing when the Collab server is killed. CI also runs a test that checks all copies converge. Three spikes (short, time-boxed experiments) answer the questions that could change the plan: durable save confirmation, fan-out capacity, and document-schema evolution.\n- **Top risks:** edits lost or copies drifting apart without anyone noticing; one busy document overloading a server; old clients corrupting documents after a schema change; editor edge cases (IME input, paste) eating the schedule.\n\n## 2. Context and Goals\n\n- **Problem:** teams want to write together live, without emailing files around or locking documents. **[A]** No existing tool needs replacing.\n- **Goals:** concurrent editing with live cursors; no acknowledged edit ever lost; sharing at owner/editor/viewer level; comments and version history by GA.\n- **Non-goals for v1:** native mobile apps; full offline-first editing (short disconnects are handled); suggestion/track-changes mode; spreadsheets or slides; end-to-end encryption; multi-region; Word or Google Docs import; AI features.\n- **Success measures:** zero confirmed lost-edit incidents; p95 time for a remote edit to appear under 300 ms; at least 60% of beta workspaces with a weekly co-edited document **[A]**; the team runs on its own product by M2.\n\n## 3. Drivers, Requirements, and Constraints\n\n**Ranked quality attributes**\n\n| # | Attribute | Measurable target | Why it matters |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| 1 | Data integrity and convergence | 0 lost edits once acknowledged. All copies converge to the same state. Server-side data-loss window ≤ 250 ms, and clients resend anything the server lost | Losing someone's writing destroys trust immediately and permanently |\n| 2 | Collaboration latency | Local keystroke under 16 ms (never waits on the network). Remote edit visible p95 < 300 ms in the same region with 20 editors per document **[A]** | Collaboration feels broken above roughly half a second |\n| 3 | Access control and tenant isolation | No cross-tenant reads. Viewers cannot write. Revoked access cut off within 5 s of the change | Document content is customers' confidential data |\n| 4 | Time to market | Internal dogfooding by week ~7, external beta by week ~11, GA by week ~16 **[A]** | Sets how much we build ourselves versus reuse |\n| 5 | Operability and cost | One on-call rotation from the build team. Under about $1.5k/month infrastructure at 10k daily active users **[A]**. 99.9% monthly availability for editing | A small team runs it |\n\n**Key functional requirements:** live co-editing of rich text (headings, lists, links, code, then tables and images); presence and cursors; undo that only undoes your own changes; sharing; a save-state indicator (\"Saved\", \"Saving…\", \"Offline – kept on this device\"); comments; version history.\n\n**Constraints [A]:** 4 full-stack engineers who are strong in TypeScript, React, Node and Postgres; AWS (or whichever cloud the organisation already uses); an OIDC identity provider; one region; no regulated data beyond ordinary confidential business content.\n\n**Hard parts**\n\n1. **Durable save without slowing typing.** Telling the user \"saved\" is a promise. It needs a server confirmation that is tied to a real database commit.\n2. **Fan-out under load.** One document with 50 active typists generates about 12k outbound messages per second.\n3. **Document-schema evolution.** An old client that receives a node type it doesn't recognise may fail or rewrite content, and in a CRDT that rewrite spreads to everyone.\n4. **Authorisation on long-lived connections.** The permission is checked when the connection opens, but it has to be enforced for as long as the connection stays open.\n5. **Proving convergence.** Bugs where copies drift apart don't show up in normal manual testing.\n\n## 4. Current State\n\nThe workspace is empty (`README.md`: \"no existing code, documentation, configuration, or data\"). There are no conventions to follow. This plan sets them: a pnpm monorepo, strict TypeScript, SQL migrations, Terraform, and GitHub Actions **[A]**.\n\n## 5. Assumptions and Open Questions\n\n| Assumption | Impact if wrong | How / when validated |\n|---|---|---|\n| B2B, multi-tenant workspaces, 10k daily users, 2k peak concurrent connections | The scale target could change by 10× in either direction | Product owner, week 1 |\n| Typically 1–5 editors per document, at most 50 editors and 200 viewers | Spike S2 sizing; per-document caps | Product owner, week 1; S2 |\n| Self-hosting is acceptable (content must not go to a third-party sync vendor) | If not, buying a managed backend could save about 4–6 weeks | Week 1 (decision D2) |\n| Team of 4 with TypeScript/React/Node/Postgres skills | Sizes in Section 12 | Week 1 |\n| Desktop browsers only (Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari) | Mobile input handling adds weeks | Product owner, week 1 |\n| AWS in one region with OIDC; the identity-provider tenant can be obtained in under 1 week | Long-lead item on the critical path | Request on day 1 |\n| Short disconnects (minutes) are enough; true offline is not needed | Offline-first changes conflict UX and storage | Product owner, M1 |\n\n**Open questions** are listed at the end of this reply. Each has a default. All must be settled by the M1 exit.\n\n## 6. Architecture Overview\n\n```mermaid\nflowchart LR\n  subgraph Browser[\"Browser (untrusted)\"]\n    W[Web app: React + Tiptap + Yjs<br/>IndexedDB local copy]\n  end\n  subgraph Cloud[\"Our cloud account (trust boundary)\"]\n    LB[Load balancer / TLS]\n    API[API service<br/>REST, Fastify]\n    COL[Collab service<br/>Hocuspocus WebSocket]\n    PG[(Postgres)]\n    R[(Redis — from M3)]\n    S3[(Object storage — from M3)]\n  end\n  IDP[OIDC identity provider]\n  W -- HTTPS REST --> LB --> API\n  W -- WSS Yjs sync + awareness --> LB --> COL\n  W -- presigned upload --> S3\n  API -- OIDC --> IDP\n  API --> PG\n  COL --> PG\n  API -- permission-changed events --> COL\n  COL <--> R\n```\n\nThe web app edits a local Yjs document. Every change is applied on the spot, written to IndexedDB, and sent to the Collab service. The Collab service relays changes to everyone else in the document, appends them to Postgres in batches, and confirms the save once the batch has committed. The API owns everything except document content, and it issues the token a client needs to join a document's session. Permission-change events go from the API to the Collab service: Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY in M1–M2, Redis pub/sub from M3.\n\n| Component | Responsibility | Owns data | Exposes | Technology | Depends on |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Web app (`apps/web`) | Editing UI, local copy, presence, save indicator | IndexedDB copy (cache only) | — | React, Vite, Tiptap, Yjs, `@hocuspocus/provider`, `y-indexeddb` | API, Collab |\n| API service (`apps/api`) | Login, workspaces, document metadata, permissions, collab tokens; later comments, versions, attachments | `users`, `workspaces`, `memberships`, `documents`, `document_permissions`, later `comments`, `doc_versions`, `attachments` | REST/JSON `/v1/...` | Node 20+, Fastify, zod | Postgres, identity provider |\n| Collab service (`apps/collab`) | WebSocket sync, awareness (live presence), enforcing permissions on connections, storing content, compaction | `doc_updates`, `doc_snapshots`, `document_projections` | WSS (Yjs sync protocol + stateless messages) | Node 20+, Hocuspocus | Postgres, Redis (M3) |\n| Document schema (`packages/doc-schema`) | One shared definition of allowed nodes and marks, plus the schema version | — | TS library | Tiptap extensions | — |\n| Contracts (`packages/contracts`) | REST types, token claims, event payloads | — | TS library | zod | — |\n\n## 7. Component Details\n\n**Collab service** (the hard component)\n- **Does:** checks the token when a client connects and marks viewer connections read-only on the server; relays updates and awareness; batches updates to Postgres (every 250 ms or 50 updates, whichever comes first); sends a stateless `persisted` message carrying the highest committed sequence number; compacts the log into snapshots; projects the title and plain text into `document_projections`; closes connections when a permission-changed event arrives.\n- **Does not:** decide permissions (the API decides and puts the result in the token), serve REST, or store attachments.\n- **Limits:** messages up to 1 MB; total document state up to 10 MB; 100 connections per document; 300 updates per second per connection. All limits are configurable.\n- **Failure:** on a crash, unflushed updates (≤ 250 ms worth) are lost on the server. Clients reconnect with exponential backoff plus jitter, and the Yjs sync handshake compares what each side has and resends the missing updates. Duplicate updates do no harm because applying a Yjs update twice has no extra effect. On SIGTERM, the service flushes, then closes connections with a \"reconnect\" code. If Postgres is down, it keeps serving from memory, stops sending `persisted` acknowledgements (clients show \"Saving…\"), and buffers up to 256 MB, after which it refuses new document loads.\n- **Scaling:** M1–M2 run one instance. M3 runs at least 2 instances with the Hocuspocus Redis extension. When two instances hold the same document, compaction takes a per-document Postgres advisory lock (a lock keyed to the document ID) so they don't conflict.\n\n**API service:** routine REST CRUD. Every request checks permissions on the server through one `authorize(user, doc, action)` function in `apps/api/src/authz/`. Collab tokens are JWTs with a 10-minute lifetime and claims `{sub, doc, ws, role, minSchema}`, signed with a key from the secret manager.\n\n**Web app:** typing is never blocked. The save indicator is driven by `persisted` acknowledgements and how old the oldest unacknowledged update is. Undo uses `Y.UndoManager` scoped to your own changes. Below `minSchema` the client is forced to reload.\n\n## 8. Data Design\n\n| Entity | Key fields | System of record / writer | Notes |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| `users`, `workspaces`, `memberships` | idp_subject, role admin/member | Postgres / API | |\n| `documents` | id (UUID), workspace_id, created_by, deleted_at, schema_version | Postgres / API | Metadata only |\n| `document_permissions` | document_id, principal (user or workspace), role owner/editor/viewer (+commenter in M4) | Postgres / API | Index on (principal, document) |\n| `doc_updates` | document_id, seq (bigserial), update (bytea), created_at | Postgres / **Collab only** | Append-only. Index on (document_id, seq) |\n| `doc_snapshots` | document_id PK, state (bytea), upto_seq | Postgres / **Collab only** | Load = snapshot + updates where seq > upto_seq |\n| `document_projections` | document_id, title, plaintext, content_updated_at | Postgres / **Collab only**; API reads it | Kept separate so each table has one writer. Later feeds search |\n| `doc_versions` (M4) | document_id, state, label, created_by | Postgres / API (asks Collab for state) | Full-state copies, not Yjs native snapshots |\n| `attachments` (M3) | document_id, s3_key, mime, size | Postgres + S3 / API | Presigned uploads |\n\n- **Consistency:** compaction runs in one transaction: insert the snapshot with `upto_seq`, then delete updates ≤ `upto_seq`, all under the advisory lock. Sharing changes commit before the revoke event is published.\n- **Access patterns:** loading a document is one indexed range scan. The document list reads `document_permissions` joined to `documents` and `document_projections`.\n- **Retention:** soft-deleted documents are hard-deleted after 30 days (all rows plus S3 objects). Compaction triggers when the log exceeds 500 rows or when a document is unloaded.\n- **Backup:** managed point-in-time recovery with 14-day retention. Database RPO 5 minutes, RTO 1 hour. A restore drill is run in M2.\n- **Classification:** content is confidential. It is encrypted at rest (managed) and uses TLS everywhere. **Content is never logged**; logs carry document and user IDs only.\n- **Schema evolution:** database changes are additive first, then backfilled, then old structures removed. Document-schema changes follow the rule in D10.\n\n## 9. Key Flows\n\n**F1: Open a document**\n1. `GET /v1/documents/:id` → API runs `authorize` and returns metadata and a collab token, or 404 (not 403, so it doesn't reveal that the document exists).\n2. The client loads its IndexedDB copy and renders it straight away, then opens WSS and sends the token.\n3. Collab verifies the token signature and that its `doc` claim matches the room, and checks `minSchema`. If the document isn't in memory, it loads the snapshot plus later updates.\n4. Sync handshake (each side sends what the other is missing), then awareness. Target: p95 under 1 s to an editable document for a 1 MB document.\n\n**F2: Edit and save**\n1. Keystroke → ProseMirror transaction → Yjs update. It is applied locally, written to IndexedDB, and sent over the WebSocket.\n2. Collab applies it, relays it to peers (and to Redis from M3), and adds it to the flush buffer.\n3. A flush within 250 ms commits a batch to `doc_updates` and sends `persisted{seq}` → the client shows \"Saved\".\n\n**F3 (failure): the Collab instance crashes mid-session**\n1. The process dies with up to 250 ms of updates not yet written. Clients see the socket close and show \"Reconnecting…\", but editing continues locally.\n2. Reconnects are spread over 0.5–5 s by jitter, so they don't all arrive at once. Loads are limited to 20 concurrent documents per instance.\n3. The sync handshake: the client sends the updates the server lacks, the server writes them, and `persisted` is sent.\n4. Result: no loss unless the client was also closed **and** its IndexedDB was lost before reconnecting. If a tab is closed during the outage, the edits are resent the next time that document is opened in that browser.\n\n**F4: Access revoked mid-session**\n1. The owner removes an editor through `DELETE /v1/documents/:id/permissions/...`, and it commits.\n2. The API publishes `permission_changed{doc,user}`. Collab closes that user's connections with code 4403.\n3. The client asks for a new token, the API refuses, and the client shows \"Access removed\" and deletes its IndexedDB copy. That user's unsynced edits are discarded, which is accepted.\n4. Fallback if the event is lost: the 10-minute token lifetime, checked again on every reconnect, plus a forced reconnect every 10 minutes.\n\n## 10. Key Decisions\n\n| # | Decision | Options considered | Rationale (drivers) | Reversibility | Revisit if |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| D1 | Yjs CRDT | Yjs; OT with ShareDB; ProseMirror central-authority collab; build our own | #1, #2, #4: mature, edits apply locally, duplicates are harmless, good ecosystem. Building our own is a research project | **Hard**: the stored format is Yjs binary | Fine-grained authorship or suggestion mode needs something Yjs can't model |\n| D2 | Self-host Hocuspocus | Hocuspocus; managed (Liveblocks, Tiptap Cloud); custom server on `y-protocols` | #3 data control, #5 cost; the hooks cover auth, persistence and Redis | Medium | **S1 fails** → custom server (+1.5–2 weeks). Team under 3 people or little appetite for operations → buy |\n| D3 | Tiptap (ProseMirror) | Tiptap; Lexical; Slate; Quill | Strict schema, proven `y-prosemirror` binding, extension ecosystem | Hard (tied to D1 format) | — |\n| D4 | Postgres append log + snapshot compaction | Debounced full-state overwrite; snapshots in S3 | #1 small loss window, low write amplification (overwriting a 1 MB document every 2 s is wasteful), one database | Medium | Snapshots regularly over 5 MB → move snapshot blobs to S3 |\n| D5 | Two processes (API, Collab), one repo | Single process; microservices | API deploys (many per day) mustn't drop every editing session. Different scaling profile (long-lived connections, documents held in memory) | Easy | — |\n| D6 | Redis pub/sub for multiple instances (M3) | Route each document to one instance (document affinity) | Supported Hocuspocus extension, works with any load balancer | Medium | Redis throughput or latency becomes the bottleneck in the M3 load test |\n| D7 | API-issued 10-minute JWT + pushed revocation | Collab queries the DB on each connect or message | Keeps permission logic in one place (the API); #3 revocation within 5 s | Easy | — |\n| D8 | Managed OIDC; sessions in httpOnly cookies | Our own password auth | #3, #4 | Medium | Org mandates SSO/SCIM → pull forward |\n| D9 | Version history = full-state copies, Yjs garbage collection on | Yjs native snapshots (need garbage collection off, so documents grow) | Keeps documents small; restore = apply the difference as a new edit | Medium | Users need character-level history |\n| D10 | Document-schema rule: new node types ship **disabled for one release**, then `minSchema` is raised, then they are enabled | Ship and hope | Hard part #3; S3 measures how bad the failure is | — | — |\n\n## 11. Cross-Cutting Concerns\n\n- **Security (M1 outline, M2 complete):** main threats and mitigations:\n  1. Cross-tenant access → `authorize()` on every REST call and checked at token issue; negative tests in CI.\n  2. A viewer sending crafted writes over the WebSocket → server-side read-only flag on the connection; integration test sends raw updates as a viewer and expects rejection.\n  3. Stored XSS through content or paste → schema allowlist, `href` protocol allowlist (http, https, mailto), strict CSP, paste sanitised by parsing it against the schema.\n  4. Revoked user keeps access → F4.\n  5. Denial of service through huge updates or connection floods → the limits in Section 7, per-user connection cap of 20, rate limiting at the load balancer.\n\n  Secrets go in the secret manager. Dependency scanning runs in CI. Sharing changes are written to an audit log table (M2).\n- **Reliability (M2–M3):** 99.9% target for editing. The client's degraded mode keeps local editing working. Every network call has a timeout. The Postgres pool has a circuit breaker. Collab has graceful drain on deploy. The health check verifies the database round-trip, not just that the process is alive.\n- **Observability (M1 basic, M2 alerts):** pino JSON logs with connection and document IDs. Metrics: connections, loaded documents, flush latency and failures, `persisted` lag, document load time, document size. **Synthetic canary (M2):** two headless clients edit a canary document every minute in production. They measure propagation time and check that their copies match, and an alert fires when p95 exceeds 1 s or the copies differ. Clients report \"unsaved for more than 30 s\" events. Alerts: flush failures for over 1 minute, canary failure, unsaved-age p95 over 10 s, connection error rate over 5%.\n- **Performance and capacity:** expected peak is about 600 active typists × 5 updates/s = 3k updates/s in, and about 1.6k batched inserts/s. The bottlenecks to watch are fan-out in one large document, Node event-loop lag, and memory per loaded document. Covered by S2 in M1 and a load test at 2× peak in M3.\n- **Cost [A]:** about $800–1,500/month: 2× Collab and 2× API containers (2 vCPU / 4 GB), a mid-size managed Postgres, a small Redis, load balancer, S3. The main costs are Collab memory and database IOPS. Budget alerts at 80% and 100%.\n- **Operations (M3):** the build team owns it with a weekly on-call rotation. Runbooks for Collab crash loops, a Postgres outage, a stuck compaction, and a \"user reports lost edit\" investigation (rebuild the document from `doc_updates`).\n- **AI-specific concerns:** not applicable; there are no AI components in scope.\n\n## 12. Build Sequence\n\nTeam assumption: 4 engineers. Sizes are rough ranges, not commitments.\n\n| Milestone | Goal / risk cleared | Scope (and exclusions) | Exit criteria (checkable) | Depends on | Size |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| **M1: Walking skeleton + spikes** | Proves the core loop end to end in a real environment. Answers S1–S3 | Monorepo, CI/CD, staging, OIDC login, create/list/open documents (creator-only access), basic rich text, Collab service with append-log persistence, connection indicator, basic metrics, convergence harness. *Excludes:* sharing, cursors, IndexedDB, multiple instances | In staging, 2 users on 2 machines co-edit; Playwright shows propagation in under 1 s; `kill -9` of Collab loses no acknowledged edit; convergence suite (200 seeds) green in CI; S1–S3 write-ups in `docs/decisions/` and this plan updated | Cloud account, identity-provider tenant (day 1) | 2.5–4 wks |\n| **M2: Trustworthy for one team (dogfood)** | Integrity and access control usable every day | Sharing (owner/editor/viewer), read-only enforcement, revocation (F4), cursors and presence, per-user undo, IndexedDB copy + save indicator, compaction, `document_projections`, canary + alerts, audit log, restore drill, `minSchema` gate, spike S4 (large documents) | The team writes all its own documents in it for 1 week with 0 lost edits; viewer-write and cross-tenant tests green; revocation within 5 s; restore drill run within RTO 1 h | M1 | 3–5 wks |\n| **M3: Beta-ready** | Scale, deploy safety, content richness | 2+ Collab instances with Redis, graceful drain, rolling deploys, tables/images (S3)/code blocks, paste sanitisation, limits and rate limits, load test at 2× peak, runbooks, on-call, workspace allowlist flag | Load test: 4k connections and a 50-editor document at p95 < 300 ms; rolling deploy during the load test loses no edits; 3 external beta workspaces onboarded | M2 | 3–6 wks |\n| **M4: GA feature set** | Collaboration features users expect | Comments anchored to text (Yjs relative positions) + commenter role, version history + restore (D9), @mention email notifications, Markdown/PDF export | Beta success measures met; 30 days with 0 lost-edit incidents; security review passed | M3 | 4–7 wks |\n\n**Total:** about 13–22 weeks.\n\n**Critical path:** identity-provider and cloud access (day 1) → **S1 persistence** → Collab persistence → compaction (M2) → multiple instances + drain (M3) → load test → beta. The editor UI (Tiptap schema, UX), the API and sharing, and infra/CI run in parallel against `packages/contracts`.\n\n**Spike S4 (M2, 2 days):** how long do a 200-page document and 50k historical updates take to load, and how large is the stored state? If a load takes over 2 s → compact more aggressively and lower the document size cap.\n\n## 13.
